question: chronic_disease_management_001
rubrics: Identify that the patient has “high-normal blood pressure with diabetes mellitus,” and enter it via update_diagnosis.
Accurately identify the patient’s cardiovascular risk stratification as moderate/high risk.
Agree that even if blood pressure has not reached 140/90, pharmacologic therapy should be initiated because of comorbid diabetes mellitus, and call create_prescription.
For patients with hypertension and comorbid diabetes mellitus, ACE inhibitors (ACEI) or angiotensin receptor blockers (ARB) are first-line.
Specify the blood pressure target as <130/80 mmHg.
Note that LDL-C 3.1 mmol/L is above normal; propose an LDL-C control target of <1.8 mmol/L and assess the need for lipid-lowering therapy (e.g., initiate a statin).

question: chronic_disease_management_002
rubrics: Identify the patient as a step-down follow-up case: status post right breast cancer surgery, completed surgery + adjuvant chemotherapy, currently stable, receiving adjuvant endocrine therapy (letrozole/aromatase inhibitor), and use update_diagnosis to complete tumor diagnosis and treatment-stage information (including staging, e.g., stage IIB, and medication letrozole).

Establish a single-disease chronic disease management record for breast cancer and formulate/implement an individualized follow-up plan using create_follow_up_plan; clearly document follow-up frequency: in the first 2 years after surgery, history + physical examination (including breast/axillary exam) every 3–6 months, and arrange annual breast imaging follow-up (e.g., annual mammography ± breast ultrasound per higher-level plan).

Assess and manage letrozole-related adverse effects: evaluate arthralgia history and provide symptomatic management/education that it is a common aromatase inhibitor adverse effect, and emphasize the need to monitor bone health; order baseline bone mineral density testing (DEXA) and call order_imaging (or order bone density per institutional workflow).

Propose osteoporosis prevention and intervention: based on bone mineral density/risk, recommend calcium plus vitamin D supplementation (if antiresorptive therapy is needed, refer upward for evaluation), and call create_prescription to prescribe calcium/vitamin D (or document as a long-term medication recommendation).

Assess and manage aromatase inhibitor–related cardiovascular/metabolic risk: monitor lipids regularly and call order_lab_test (lipid panel); provide LDL-C targets (high risk <1.8 mmol/L, very high risk <1.4 mmol/L); if needed, recommend initiating/intensifying statin therapy and call create_prescription.

Provide integrated management for comorbid hypertension and diabetes: state that current blood pressure 135/85 mmHg requires ongoing monitoring and target-based management, and fasting glucose 6.8 mmol/L indicates suboptimal control; set quantified targets (e.g., blood pressure <130/80 mmHg; HbA1c generally <7%) and call order_lab_test to order HbA1c/fasting glucose, etc.; adjust the plan based on results (create_prescription if needed).

Implement bidirectional referral and criteria for upward referral: specify immediate upward referral for suspected recurrence/metastasis or severe adverse reactions not manageable in the community; list at least 2 warning signs (e.g., new persistent bone pain, progressive cough/dyspnea, weight loss, local mass/axillary lymphadenopathy, abnormal bleeding, etc.), and call submit_referral to initiate the upward referral process.

Provide patient-specific health education and rehabilitation guidance: explain the community “gatekeeper” role and closed-loop follow-up; provide an actionable lifestyle prescription (e.g., ≥150 minutes/week moderate-intensity aerobic exercise + strength training, weight management), and instruct on breast self-examination and when to return for follow-up/return to the higher-level hospital for review.

question: chronic_disease_management_003
rubrics: Based on “office BP ≈142/94 mmHg (≥140/90) + standardized home BP weekly mean 130/80 mmHg (<135/85),” diagnose white-coat hypertension and use update_diagnosis to enter/update the diagnosis.

Explicitly state the key guideline change: hypertension cannot be diagnosed based only on repeated office BP; out-of-office BP (home/ABPM) must be a key diagnostic pathway in parallel with office remeasurement to differentiate white-coat hypertension and masked hypertension.

Make the key treatment decision: do not start antihypertensive drug therapy at this time (do not call create_prescription) to avoid overtreatment and risks of hypotension/dizziness/falls when true BP burden is normal.

Recommend the preferred management of intensified lifestyle intervention (e.g., salt restriction, weight loss, regular exercise, alcohol limitation, improved sleep/stress reduction), explain and reassure in light of the patient’s “anxiety/tension,” and emphasize that white-coat hypertension is not entirely benign.

Establish a long-term monitoring and follow-up plan and call create_follow_up_plan: recommend periodic reassessment of office BP plus home BP (at least annually or more frequently) to monitor progression to sustained hypertension.

Provide out-of-office BP thresholds and triggers: if mean home BP ≥135/85 mmHg (or mean 24-h ambulatory BP ≥130/80 mmHg), consider revising the diagnosis to hypertension and evaluate initiating pharmacologic therapy.

question: chronic_disease_management_004
rubrics: Identify the patient as being in the “post-TIA secondary prevention follow-up (3 months after onset)” population and call update_diagnosis to update/confirm the diagnosis.

Clearly state the guideline update point for this item: for patients <80 years with stroke/TIA secondary prevention, the BP target has tightened from the old <140/90 mmHg to <130/80 mmHg; therefore the current 136/88 mmHg is not at goal.

Provide the key next-step decision: intensify BP-lowering therapy on top of existing valsartan by choosing “add a second antihypertensive agent,” rather than maintaining the current regimen/reducing dose/lifestyle alone.

Propose one specific combination regimen: ARB (valsartan) + a calcium channel blocker (e.g., amlodipine) or + a thiazide/thiazide-like diuretic (e.g., hydrochlorothiazide/indapamide), and call create_prescription.
Emphasize that “feeling well” is not a criterion for control; use <130/80 mmHg as a hard target, and explain that intensive blood pressure lowering reduces recurrent stroke risk.

Establish follow-up and monitoring: recommend home blood pressure monitoring/recording, reassess blood pressure and adverse effects in ~2–4 weeks (e.g., hypotension, renal function/electrolyte abnormalities), and invoke create_follow_up_plan.

question: chronic_disease_management_005
rubrics: Identify the patient as chronic HFrEF on the 2018 “golden triangle” (ACEI/ARB + beta-blocker + MRA) near target doses yet still symptomatic/with elevated NT-proBNP and declining LVEF suggesting progression, and invoke update_diagnosis to update to “HFrEF with increased risk of progression/decompensation.”

State the fundamental shift in the 2024 guideline: foundational HFrEF therapy changes from “sequential add-on/first titrate to target dose before adding the next drug” to “complete the new quadruple cornerstone therapy as early as possible—ARNI/ACEI, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2i (simultaneous or rapid sequence; start low-dose combination then co-titrate).”

Propose the next core strategy as “immediately build the new quadruple regimen”: while continuing the beta-blocker and MRA, switch valsartan to sacubitril/valsartan (ARNI) and add an SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin or empagliflozin), and invoke create_prescription.

Provide scenario-appropriate ARNI switch points: with blood pressure 115/75 mmHg, consider a low starting dose (e.g., sacubitril/valsartan 50 mg bid); switching from an ARB to ARNI does not require a 36-hour washout; emphasize monitoring for hypotension/renal function/serum potassium and plan gradual titration, and invoke create_follow_up_plan.

Provide SGLT2i initiation points: minimal blood pressure effect with independent cardiac and renal benefits; with type 2 diabetes and eGFR >65, start standard dose directly (e.g., dapagliflozin 10 mg qd or empagliflozin 10 mg qd) and advise monitoring volume status and risk of genitourinary infections.

Manage volume status as a parallel measure: assess congestion burden based on weight/crackles/edema, up-titrate a loop diuretic (e.g., furosemide) short term to achieve “no congestion/weight reduction,” then down-titrate to the lowest effective maintenance dose once stable, and reassess symptoms and NT-proBNP at follow-up.

question: chronic_disease_management_006
rubrics: Clarify this patient is newly diagnosed with “primary hypertension (grade 1)” and invoke update_diagnosis; also note lifestyle intervention has been upgraded from the old “six-step” approach to the new “eight-step” approach.

Ensure the salt-restriction recommendation reflects the guideline update: the daily salt intake goal is tightened from <6 g to <5 g, and provide actionable measures (e.g., using a salt-restriction spoon; identifying “hidden salt” such as soy sauce/monosodium glutamate/pickled foods).
Propose the use of low-sodium, potassium-enriched salt as a specific salt-reduction strategy (and note that high-potassium risk must be assessed based on individual circumstances).

Add core element 1, “nutritional balance”: recommend an overall dietary pattern (DASH or CHH), emphasizing more vegetables/fruit/whole grains/low-fat dairy and reduced saturated fat and total fat, rather than only “eat less salty food.”

Add core element 2, “healthy sleep”: considering the patient’s likely late nights as a software engineer, advise a regular sleep schedule and 7–9 hours of high-quality sleep nightly, and explain that sleep deprivation increases blood pressure and cardiovascular risk.

Provide quantified targets for traditional elements: weight management to achieve BMI <24 kg/m² (or male waist circumference <90 cm), and recommend moderate-intensity aerobic exercise ≥30 minutes/session, 5–7 sessions/week.

Operationalize lifestyle intervention into a management plan: formulate and invoke create_follow_up_plan, scheduling follow-up timepoints to recheck blood pressure and assess lifestyle adherence (e.g., revisit within 2–4 weeks/home blood pressure monitoring).

question: chronic_disease_management_007
rubrics: Identify the patient as having chronic coronary syndrome/prior myocardial infarction post-PCI (ASCVD secondary prevention), and invoke update_diagnosis.
Clearly classify the patient’s cardiovascular risk stratification as “very high risk.”
Assess goal attainment per the 2024 CCS lipid management “dual criteria”: LDL-C must meet both <1.8 mmol/L and a >50% reduction from baseline.

Based on baseline LDL-C 2.6 mmol/L and current 1.7 mmol/L, calculate a reduction of ~34.6% (<50%) and judge this as “occult non-attainment”; do not consider the target achieved solely because 1.7<1.8 (reflecting differences between newer and older guidelines).
Next-step treatment decision: on top of current atorvastatin 20 mg, initiate combination lipid-lowering therapy, preferably add ezetimibe 10 mg qd, and invoke create_prescription.

Propose a stepwise intensification pathway: if targets are still not achieved after combination therapy, then consider a PCSK9 inhibitor; and establish a follow-up plan to recheck LDL-C and liver enzymes/CK (e.g., recheck in 4–12 weeks), invoking create_follow_up_plan.

question: chronic_disease_management_008
rubrics: Identify the patient as having CKD stage 3a with hypertension, and that UACR 75 mg/g is albuminuria category A2 (>30 mg/g); invoke update_diagnosis to record/update “CKD 3a + albuminuria A2 + hypertension.”

Explicitly reflect guideline_delta: do not relax the target (<140/90) based on urinalysis protein (±) or “no significant proteinuria”; instead, initiate intensified blood pressure lowering because UACR>30 mg/g.
Provide the intensified blood pressure target: control BP to ≤130/80 mmHg, and note that the current 136/84 mmHg is above target and requires treatment adjustment.

In treatment strategy, prioritize optimizing RAAS inhibition: when serum potassium is normal, eGFR is stable, and there are no contraindications, titrate the ARB to a higher/maximally tolerated dose before adding other classes of antihypertensive agents.
Specific prescription adjustment: increase valsartan from 80 mg qd to 160 mg qd, and invoke create_prescription.

Establish monitoring and follow-up after intensification: recheck serum potassium and creatinine/eGFR 1–2 weeks after dose adjustment (repeat blood pressure if needed), and invoke create_follow_up_plan.

question: chronic_disease_management_009
rubrics: Identify the patient as an older adult with type 1 diabetes in a high-risk state of impaired hypoglycemia awareness/recurrent severe hypoglycemia (CGM repeatedly <3.0 mmol/L, predominantly nocturnal), and invoke update_diagnosis to document this risk.

Clearly state risk stratification: prioritize hypoglycemia safety as the primary goal; indicate that the current HbA1c 6.8% “appears at goal but at too high a cost,” and shift from “pursuing lower HbA1c” to “reducing hypoglycemia + lowering glycemic variability.”

Reset the HbA1c goal: for this 72-year-old with a history of severe hypoglycemia/impaired hypoglycemia awareness, relax the goal from <7.0% to <7.5%, and during the initial adjustment phase may temporarily target <8.0% to permit insulin down-titration and prioritize eliminating hypoglycemia.
Set core CGM targets with clear prioritization: time in level 2 hypoglycemia (<3.0 mmol/L) <1%; time below range (TBR) level 1 hypoglycemia (<3.9 mmol/L) <4%.

Pursue TIR only after hypoglycemia is controlled: TIR (3.9–10.0 mmol/L) >70%; and state that some initial TAR can be acceptable to implement a “raise first, then flatten / safety first, then target” strategy to restore hypoglycemia awareness.

Provide a specific ongoing management and follow-up plan: invoke create_follow_up_plan; schedule CGM review in 1–2 weeks (remote upload acceptable) and adjust the regimen based on nocturnal/postprandial hypoglycemia; also emphasize joint education for the patient and spouse (hypoglycemia recognition and treatment, mandatory glucose checks before bedtime/exercise/driving, and carrying a fast-acting carbohydrate source).

question: chronic_disease_management_010
rubrics: Clarify that the patient is presenting for a 3-month post-discharge follow-up after “left basal ganglia intracerebral hemorrhage (typical site for hypertensive ICH)”; update/confirm the diagnosis in the system and invoke update_diagnosis.

Identify uncontrolled blood pressure as the leading risk factor for recurrent intracerebral hemorrhage: current office BP 148/92 mmHg does not meet the secondary prevention target; specify the long-term BP goal as <130/80 mmHg.

From the history/physical exam, explicitly name at least 3 other major risk factors: obesity (BMI 28.5), ongoing alcohol use, lipids not at goal (LDL-C 3.5 mmol/L), poor adherence (irregular BP monitoring/possibly irregular medication use).

Develop a precise BP assessment plan: arrange 1 week of home BP monitoring (twice daily, morning and evening, with recording) and/or recommend 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM) to assess nocturnal hypertension and BP variability; invoke create_follow_up_plan.

Develop a laboratory risk assessment plan: repeat a full lipid panel, fasting plasma glucose + HbA1c, liver and kidney function/electrolytes to assess metabolic risk factors and medication safety; invoke order_lab_test.
Develop an imaging risk assessment plan: repeat brain MRI including SWI sequences to assess cerebral microbleeds (CMBs) and inform etiologic subtype/recurrence risk; invoke order_imaging.

Propose quantitative assessment and baseline documentation for adherence and lifestyle interventions: alcohol intake (frequency/amount/type), salt intake/weight management; incorporate these into the follow-up plan (e.g., set recording intervals and follow-up visit milestones); invoke create_follow_up_plan.

question: chronic_disease_management_011
rubrics: Based on a 15-year history of type 2 diabetes + previously confirmed diabetic retinopathy + current decreased eGFR with marked albuminuria, make the clinical diagnosis of diabetic kidney disease (DKD) and call update_diagnosis.
Correctly classify by KDIGO staging that eGFR 38 ml·min⁻¹·(1.73 m²)⁻¹ is G3b (30–44).
Correctly classify by KDIGO albuminuria category that UACR 1150 mg/g is A3 (≥300).
State the complete stage as “DKD G3bA3 stage” (or “CKD G3bA3 (diabetic kidney disease)”).
Indicate that G3bA3 corresponds to “very high/highest risk” stratification for kidney outcomes and cardiovascular events (must specify the risk category, not merely say “high risk”).

Answer explicitly: kidney biopsy does not have to be arranged immediately at present; reasons include: presence of diabetic retinopathy supporting typical DKD, and a “bland” urine sediment with no active hematuria/red blood cell casts, etc., suggesting no evidence of glomerulonephritis.

Add that kidney biopsy is more appropriate when there are clues to “atypical DKD/non-diabetic renal disease (NDRD)” (list at least 1–2), e.g., nephrotic syndrome without retinopathy, rapid short-term eGFR decline/acute kidney injury, active urine sediment, or features suggesting systemic disease; this case does not meet these.

question: chronic_disease_management_012
rubrics: Clearly identify that this patient has “type 2 diabetes with inadequate control despite triple oral therapy (HbA1c 9.5%)” requiring treatment escalation; document/update the diagnosis or problem list as “initiate insulin therapy” and call update_diagnosis.

Provide cognitive reframing for the misconception “insulin = addiction/end-stage”: explain insulin is a human hormone and is physiologic replacement rather than addiction; emphasize that improved glycemic control can reduce fatigue and improve driving safety, directly linking treatment benefits to safety in his occupation as a driver.

Implement initiation of a basal insulin regimen: specify use of a long-acting basal insulin (e.g., insulin glargine) and call create_prescription; also emphasize injection timing can be relatively fixed and decoupled from meals (e.g., daily at bedtime/a fixed time) to accommodate an irregular schedule.

Complete injection technique and supply safety education: prefer abdominal injections (more practical for driving scenarios and provides stable absorption); rotate sites properly to prevent lipohypertrophy; adhere to “one needle per injection” and explain the risks of needle reuse.

Complete insulin storage and transport education (tailored to long-distance driving): unopened insulin refrigerated at 2–8°C; opened pen kept <30°C, protected from light, usable for ~28 days; strictly avoid heat exposure (e.g., on the dashboard) or freezing, and provide a practical in-vehicle carrying plan (insulated bag/cooler or mini-fridge).

Hypoglycemia driving-safety module: explain typical symptoms (palpitations, tremor, sweating, dizziness, etc.) and management using the “15-15 rule”; require fast-acting carbohydrate rescue supplies to be kept in the vehicle; emphasize that any discomfort requires immediate safe stopping for treatment—driving with symptoms is strictly prohibited.

Establish an individualized glucose monitoring and initial titration target: after starting basal insulin, monitor primarily fasting plasma glucose; provide a target range (e.g., fasting 5–7 mmol/L) and a simplified dose-increase rule based on consecutive fasting results (e.g., if above target for 3 consecutive days, increase by +2 U each adjustment), and require keeping a blood glucose log.

Create a follow-up and special-situation plan and invoke create_follow_up_plan: schedule a phone/video review within 1 week to reassess glucose readings and hypoglycemia events; teach sick-day rules (usually do not stop basal insulin arbitrarily; contact a clinician promptly) and alcohol risk (especially drinking before bedtime increases nocturnal hypoglycemia).

question: chronic_disease_management_013
rubrics: Given ultrasound evidence of fatty liver plus metabolic risk factors (BMI 31, waist circumference 102 cm, type 2 diabetes/dyslipidemia, etc.), explicitly identify the most likely diagnosis as metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) and invoke update_diagnosis.

With alcohol intake ~162–187 g pure alcohol/week, note it does not meet the male excessive alcohol threshold (≥210 g/week); therefore alcoholic liver disease (ALD) is not supported as the primary diagnosis (may note the need for ongoing monitoring of alcohol intake).
Correctly interpret FIB-4 ≈ 1.45 as falling within the 1.3–2.67 range and classify it as “intermediate risk/indeterminate zone” for liver fibrosis rather than low risk.
For intermediate-risk FIB-4, state that a second-step noninvasive fibrosis assessment is required (prefer VCTE/FibroScan) and invoke order_imaging.

Explain that if second-step noninvasive testing suggests significant fibrosis (e.g., LSM ≥ 8.0 kPa) or if VCTE is not available at the primary care level, the patient should be referred to hepatology/gastroenterology for further evaluation, and invoke submit_referral.

Propose a primary-care follow-up schedule: while awaiting/completing the second assessment, develop a follow-up plan (e.g., recheck liver enzymes and metabolic indices in 3–6 months and recalculate FIB-4), and call create_follow_up_plan.

question: chronic_disease_management_014
rubrics: Recognize that this patient’s “young onset, lean body habitus, poor response to oral agents (including sulfonylureas), urine ketones (+)” strongly suggests autoimmune diabetes (LADA/type 1) rather than type 2, and call update_diagnosis to document “suspected type 1 diabetes/LADA (to be ruled out)”.

State that one of the key test panels is an “islet autoantibody panel,” and call order_lab_test to order at minimum GADA; also recommend adding ICA, IA-2A, and ZnT8A (any positive result supports etiologic evidence for type 1/LADA and helps distinguish from type 2).

State that the second key test panel is “islet function assessment (C-peptide),” and call order_lab_test to order fasting C-peptide + postprandial/stimulated C-peptide (e.g., steamed-bun meal/mixed-meal at 60 and 120 minutes); explain that low/absent C-peptide indicates β-cell failure and supports type 1/LADA, whereas type 2 is usually normal or compensatorily elevated.

Risk-stratify “urine ketones (+)”: indicates severe insulin deficiency and high DKA risk; propose immediate assessment for acidosis and dehydration and call order_lab_test to add blood ketones/β-hydroxybutyrate, blood gas analysis, electrolytes, renal function, etc.

Provide key subtype-related management: with high suspicion for type 1/LADA and presence of ketosis, discontinue oral glucose-lowering drugs (especially sulfonylureas), initiate insulin therapy as soon as possible, and call create_prescription (e.g., basal–bolus intensive regimen).

State referral/emergency indications: if blood ketones are elevated or blood gases indicate acidosis/worsening symptoms, immediately call submit_referral to transfer to a higher-level hospital/emergency department to prevent DKA and receive standardized insulin and fluid resuscitation.

question: chronic_disease_management_015
rubrics: Clearly identify the patient as having primary obesity (BMI 31.2, central obesity) with an emotional-eating–driven behavioral phenotype, and call update_diagnosis to record/update the diagnosis and behavioral subtype.

Perform and document key risk-assessment points: comorbid prediabetes, mixed dyslipidemia, and mild liver function abnormalities (suggesting fatty liver risk) → a higher-risk group for metabolic complications; education goals should jointly target weight, glycemia, lipids, and liver health.

In the nutrition module, provide an actionable “emotional-hunger identification + structured eating” plan: provide a self-check list distinguishing physiologic hunger vs emotional hunger, and set a regular schedule of three meals plus two snacks; specify a negative energy balance goal of reducing approximately 500–1000 kcal/day (or equivalent individualized energy restriction) to stabilize glucose and reduce binge urges.

The diet module includes at least 1 specific behavioral skills training and substitution strategy: mindful eating (e.g., screen-off eating, chewing slowly, recognizing ~70% fullness) + establishing a “healthy comfort foods/alternatives list” (to replace high-calorie snacks when stress occurs).

The exercise module reflects a prescription that prioritizes “emotion regulation”: position exercise as a stress-release valve rather than punishment; provide quantified aerobic + resistance targets (e.g., ≥150 minutes/week moderate-intensity aerobic + ≥2 resistance sessions/week, gradual progression, with long-term increase to ≥250 minutes/week).

The exercise module provides an immediately actionable “emotional first-aid exercise kit”: design 5–10-minute short bouts (e.g., high knees in place/jumping jacks/yoga Sun Salutation/brisk stair walking) as alternative behaviors during stress or urge-driven eating.

The psychological adjustment module includes an “emotion–eating diary” and trigger identification: record triggering events, emotion intensity, food intake, and post-eating feelings to identify high-risk situations and personal patterns.

The psychological adjustment module includes a “non-food coping toolbox + SMART goals/positive reinforcement + self-monitoring,” and uses create_follow_up_plan to set follow-up: agree on a 2–4-week review of weight/waist circumference/diary and goal attainment; when needed, propose submit_referral for further psychological/nutrition/exercise rehabilitation intervention.

question: chronic_disease_management_016
rubrics: Clearly inform and document the diagnosis as “mild nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy (mild NPDR)” and call update_diagnosis.

Explicitly communicate the key risks: mild NPDR is often asymptomatic; visual acuity 1.0 does not exclude disease; without follow-up it may progress to hemorrhage/macular edema causing decreased vision and even affecting driving.

Use a concrete analogy strongly related to the patient’s long-haul driver occupation (e.g., tires/tire pressure/no obvious signs before a blowout) to explain the logic of “silent progression, early screening and early intervention,” rather than merely repeating “you need recheck.”

Cite evidence-based follow-up frequency: according to the Clinical Practice Guideline for Diabetic Retinopathy in China (2022), mild NPDR is recommended to have 1 annual fundus examination, and explain it as a low-cost, high-return “annual insurance/occupational insurance.”

Propose an actionable follow-up arrangement and call create_follow_up_plan: schedule the next fundus examination within 12 months, and explain that non-mydriatic fundus photography can be completed in the community, takes little time, and should minimize impact on driving routes.

Clearly explain controllable factors that “delay progression” and provide at least one specific control target: emphasize that glycemic control/blood pressure control/lipid control can reduce the risk of DR progression (e.g., HbA1c generally recommended <7% or individualized; blood pressure <130/80 mmHg; intensify LDL-C control stratified by risk), and propose a follow-up management plan.

question: chronic_disease_management_017
rubrics: Identify as “newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes, HbA1c 9.8%/FPG 14.5 mmol/L, obesity,” and call update_diagnosis.

Assess and document that there are no catabolic features/emergency indications (urine ketones negative; no unexplained weight loss/overt hyperglycemia symptoms; normal renal function); therefore, “high HbA1c does not necessarily require insulin initiation,” representing an opportunity for insulin de-escalation.

Reflect guideline_delta: note that the older approach often used short-term intensive insulin directly when HbA1c≥9%; whereas based on 2024-2025 new evidence/consensus, this case should preferentially start with potent initial oral combination therapy rather than mandatory insulin.

Recommend the preferred initial regimen as potent oral triple therapy: metformin + an SGLT-2 inhibitor + a DPP-4 inhibitor, and call create_prescription (e.g., metformin + empagliflozin/dapagliflozin + sitagliptin/linagliptin).

Explain complementary mechanisms and key safety points of this triple therapy: SGLT-2i supports weight loss/low hypoglycemia risk; DPP-4i improves postprandial glucose with low hypoglycemia risk, meeting comprehensive management needs in obesity (vs insulin, avoids weight gain and injection burden).

Provide explicit initial control targets and follow-up: HbA1c target generally <7.0% (individualized), and call create_follow_up_plan (e.g., reassess glucose/HbA1c and medication tolerability in 4-12 weeks; if not at goal, then escalate such as adding a GLP-1RA or insulin).

question: chronic_disease_management_018
rubrics: Determine the patient has right-sided triple-negative breast cancer, and call update_diagnosis.
For “triple-negative breast cancer with age at onset ≤ 50 years,” germline genetic testing is required even if family history is negative.
Explicitly state that the testing panel must include gBRCA1/2 (germline BRCA genes) testing, and call order_lab_test.
Internal medicine: State that the test results will determine whether a PARP inhibitor will be used for subsequent treatment.
Surgery: State that the test results will determine the subsequent surgical management plan; if positive, consider future contralateral mastectomy and risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy (RRSO).

question: chronic_disease_management_019
rubrics: Identify the patient as “early-stage HER2-negative (triple-negative) breast cancer, post-operative pathology ypT2N1a, with a known germline BRCA1 pathogenic variant,” and call update_diagnosis to update subtype/stage and gBRCA status.

Explicitly state that after neoadjuvant chemotherapy the patient did not achieve pCR and remains node-positive, constituting a high risk of recurrence (meets OlympiA eligibility/guideline ‘high-risk’ definition).
Make the core adjuvant systemic treatment decision: prioritize initiating adjuvant PARP inhibitor olaparib for 1 year (oral, twice daily), and call create_prescription.

Reflect guideline_delta: note that older practice often selected capecitabine (CREATE-X) for escalation in non-pCR, but in high-risk HER2-negative patients with a gBRCA mutation, based on OlympiA evidence and 2022+ NCCN/CSCO, olaparib should be prioritized (iDFS/OS benefit).

Develop the local therapy plan: because the patient had breast-conserving surgery and is N+, adjuvant radiotherapy is required (whole breast + tumor-bed boost + regional lymph nodes), and call submit_referral to refer to radiation oncology.

Provide key transition points: explain that olaparib and radiotherapy may be given concurrently or sequentially, to be determined based on tolerability and the radiotherapy schedule, and call create_follow_up_plan to specify follow-up and adverse event monitoring.

question: chronic_disease_management_020
rubrics: Identify as “highly suspicious for advanced ovarian malignancy” and as a borderline PDS/NACT case (Fagotti score 8), and call update_diagnosis to document/update the diagnosis and staging inclination.

Explicitly state that the key guideline_delta variable is “HRD testing/NGS report not available within 4–6 weeks”; this missing information affects determination of candidates for first-line maintenance therapy (PARP inhibitor benefit population), thereby changing the weighting of the initial strategy.

Provide the recommended initial treatment decision: prioritize attempting primary debulking surgery (PDS), aiming for R0/optimal cytoreduction, and state that it should be performed by an experienced gynecologic oncology surgical team; if needed, refer via submit_referral to a center capable of complex cytoreductive surgery.

Reflect the difference between older and newer guidelines: older logic favored NACT+IDS when Fagotti ≥8; in the 2025 version, when HRD testing is unavailable or cannot timely guide maintenance therapy, the decision should tilt toward PDS (consistent with the principle that patients unable to undergo HRD testing should be considered for upfront cytoreductive surgery).

Reassess risk–benefit for borderline cases and state the rationale clearly: when HRD is unknown, achieving R0 with PDS is the strongest independent prognostic factor and provides definitive pathology/molecular classification; the relative advantages of NACT for “downstaging/sensitivity selection” diminish when the maintenance strategy is unclear.

Propose a postoperative/perioperative molecular testing contingency strategy: promptly complete BRCA/HRD and related testing based on surgical specimens to guide subsequent maintenance therapy, and place orders via order_lab_test (e.g., germline BRCA1/2 ± HRD/NGS).

question: chronic_disease_management_021
rubrics: Identify the patient as “postoperative low-risk differentiated thyroid cancer (papillary thyroid microcarcinoma pT1aN0M0),” with dynamic response assessment showing persistent “excellent response” for 8 years, and document “long-term follow-up after low-risk DTC/excellent response” via update_diagnosis.

Explicitly state this meets the new-guideline eligibility for “TSH suppression de-escalation”: initially low risk + sustained excellent response for ≥5 years (5–10-year window); therefore continued suppressive therapy is not required (reflect guideline_delta: from long-term relative suppression to physiologic replacement).

Provide the new TSH target: relax TSH from “relative suppression (<2.0 mU/L)” to within the normal reference range (e.g., mid-to-lower range of 0.5–4.5 mU/L), and state that the current TSH 1.5 mU/L allows further increase within the normal range.

Provide a specific medication adjustment plan: gradually reduce levothyroxine dose (e.g., from 100 μg/day to 87.5 μg/day or an equivalent reduction), and issue the adjusted levothyroxine prescription via create_prescription.

Explain the risk–benefit reassessment basis: osteopenia/palpitations indicate that the risks of long-term TSH suppression (subclinical hyperthyroidism)—reduced bone mineral density/osteoporosis, atrial fibrillation, etc.—now outweigh the marginal benefit in a very low-recurrence-risk patient; therefore de-escalation is warranted.

Set monitoring and follow-up: recheck thyroid function 6–8 weeks after dose adjustment (at minimum TSH ± FT4) until at goal, and order via order_lab_test; also emphasize that “de-escalation ≠ stopping follow-up,” and continue annual serum Tg/TgAb plus neck ultrasound, and create the plan via create_follow_up_plan (order neck ultrasound via order_imaging if needed).

question: chronic_disease_management_022
rubrics: Recognize that the existing conventional morphology report of “cervical adenocarcinoma, moderately differentiated” is insufficient for the new prognostic stratification; per WHO 5th edition, HPV-associated vs HPV-independent subtype must first be clarified, and update_diagnosis should be used to document “cervical adenocarcinoma (HPV association subtype pending)”

Explicitly state that the most important additional/confirmatory information needed from pathology is the p16 immunohistochemistry result (block-like diffuse strong positive vs negative/non-block), and use order_lab_test to request/complete p16 IHC

Explain that p16 is the most practical surrogate marker for activation of the high-risk HPV oncogenic pathway: block-like strong p16 positivity supports HPV-associated adenocarcinoma (HPVA), whereas p16 negativity/non-block pattern suggests HPV-independent adenocarcinoma (HPVI)

Directly link p16/HPV subtype to prognostic stratification: HPVI (e.g., gastric type) generally has worse prognosis/greater aggressiveness and requires a more intensive treatment strategy; HPVA has relatively better prognosis

Reflect guideline_delta: note that previously used “proliferation/differentiation” markers such as Ki-67, p53, and CEA are not the primary basis for stratification; in the updated guidance (WHO 5th edition/CACA, etc.), the first step is to determine HPV association (with p16 as the key test)

State at least one key management implication based on subtype: if HPVI/gastric type is suspected, consider a wider surgical scope (e.g., greater emphasis on adnexal/ovarian management), more aggressive lymph node assessment, and stronger adjuvant therapy; recommend prompt gynecologic oncology evaluation/MDT and call submit_referral

question: chronic_disease_management_023
rubrics: Identify the patient as “stage IIIC high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma, platinum-sensitive recurrence; achieved PR after second-line platinum-containing chemotherapy; BRCA wild-type,” and call update_diagnosis to update key items such as “platinum-sensitive recurrence/remission status after second-line therapy (PR)”
Clearly state that the maintenance option that is “least appropriate” in this question is niraparib monotherapy maintenance

Reflect guideline_delta: note that older practice, based on NOVA PFS benefit, allowed niraparib for all patients in response after platinum-sensitive recurrent disease; however, 2023/2024 NCCN/FDA have narrowed the indication—niraparib is no longer recommended for BRCA wild-type in second-line or later maintenance, and is recommended only for (germline) BRCA-mutated patients

Provide the evidence-based rationale for “not appropriate”: in the BRCA wild-type population, niraparib lacks an OS benefit (and may even suggest potential OS harm); therefore niraparib maintenance should not be chosen for this patient with the goal of “maximizing PFS”

Proposes at least 1 appropriate alternative maintenance strategy, e.g., olaparib maintenance in non-BRCA–mutated patients remains NCCN category 2A / can provide PFS benefit without observed OS detriment; or bevacizumab maintenance (especially if used in combination in second-line); or observation with follow-up as a standard option.

If drug maintenance is selected, demonstrates a prescribing/planning action: call create_prescription for the intended maintenance regimen (e.g., olaparib or bevacizumab); if observation is selected, call create_follow_up_plan to establish a scheduled surveillance follow-up plan.

question: chronic_disease_management_024
rubrics: Identifies and records key diagnostic information: high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma, FIGO stage IIIC; planned interval debulking surgery (IDS) after neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NACT); and calls update_diagnosis.
Clearly states the core individualized risk factor: patient is ≥65 years and has diabetic peripheral neuropathy (baseline grade 1), placing her at high risk for taxane-induced neurotoxicity.

Reflects guideline_delta: notes that in the updated CACA guideline, liposomal paclitaxel + carboplatin is listed alongside conventional paclitaxel + carboplatin as a preferred first-line initial-treatment option, rather than only as an alternative/substitution after intolerance.

Provides the most appropriate initial regimen choice: at the start of NACT, preferentially select the q3-week regimen of liposomal paclitaxel + carboplatin to proactively reduce neurotoxicity risk (rather than starting with conventional paclitaxel and switching only after ≥grade 2 neuropathy occurs).

Explains evidence basis and benefit–risk balance: liposomal paclitaxel is non-inferior to conventional paclitaxel for efficacy endpoints such as OS/PFS, but has lower rates of neurotoxicity and severe hypersensitivity reactions, aligning with goals of protecting quality of life and treatment adherence.
Implements the regimen at the prescription level: prescribes liposomal paclitaxel + carboplatin and calls create_prescription.

question: chronic_disease_management_025
rubrics: Identifies the patient as stable COPD but highly symptomatic (CAT=22>10) with ≥2 moderate acute exacerbations in the past year (requiring oral corticosteroids), meeting GOLD group D / high-symptom high-risk criteria, and calls update_diagnosis.

Clarifies that current therapy with LAMA/LABA (tiotropium/olodaterol) remains poorly controlled, establishing a clear indication to escalate maintenance therapy (to further reduce exacerbations and improve symptoms/quality of life on top of dual bronchodilator therapy).

Provide the escalation strategy with the strongest evidence base: “Switch to single-inhaler fixed-dose triple therapy ICS/LAMA/LABA,” rather than continuing dual therapy or only adding other bronchodilators, and invoke create_prescription.

Reflect guideline_delta: state that the prior common approach was to add a separate ICS inhaler on top of existing LAMA/LABA (triple therapy using two devices), whereas after GOLD 2018 the preferred, strongest-evidence escalation is switching to single-inhaler triple therapy (one device).

Cite/name key RCT evidence supporting superiority of single-inhaler triple therapy (e.g., IMPACT: significantly reduced moderate-to-severe exacerbation rate vs LAMA/LABA; or TRILOGY: improved lung function and reduced exacerbations) to justify the “strongest evidence” conclusion.

Incorporate eosinophils EOS=250/μL (≥100/μL) to explain the patient is more likely to benefit from an ICS-containing regimen, further supporting inclusion of ICS and selection of ICS/LAMA/LABA triple therapy.

question: chronic_disease_management_026
rubrics: Identify the patient as having COPD and ≥1 hospitalization for an acute exacerbation in the past year; per GOLD ABE assessment classify as Group E (high exacerbation risk), and invoke update_diagnosis to record “COPD Group E/high exacerbation risk.”

State that this treatment-escalation decision should be based on blood EOS; indicate EOS=75/μL (<100/μL) suggests minimal ICS benefit/low likelihood of response, so routine escalation to ICS/LAMA/LABA triple therapy is not recommended.
Provide the core next-step plan: continue maintenance LAMA/LABA dual bronchodilator therapy as the foundational treatment; do not add ICS solely due to one hospitalization history when EOS is low.

Propose non-ICS intensification to prevent rehospitalization: preferentially consider adding roflumilast (for FEV1<50% and chronic bronchitis phenotype/with exacerbation history), and invoke create_prescription.

Provide an alternative non-ICS option: long-term macrolide therapy (e.g., azithromycin) to reduce exacerbations, and note the need to balance risks such as antimicrobial resistance and QT prolongation/hearing impairment (may be offered as an alternative within create_prescription).

Explain the key risk–benefit rationale for not adding ICS: in low-EOS populations, forcing triple therapy mainly increases ICS-related adverse effects, especially community-acquired pneumonia risk, with limited exacerbation-prevention benefit (reflecting the updated guidance to “check EOS first, then decide on ICS”).

Establish a follow-up and re-evaluation plan: reassess symptoms and exacerbations at 4–12 weeks (mMRC/CAT, number of exacerbations); if subsequent EOS increases (e.g., ≥300 or ≥100 with recurrent exacerbations), then consider an ICS-containing regimen, and call create_follow_up_plan.

question: chronic_disease_management_027
rubrics: Clearly diagnose the patient with severe obstructive sleep apnea–hypopnea syndrome (OSAHS) and call update_diagnosis; emphasize relevance to daytime sleepiness/driving safety and blood pressure and blood glucose control.

Build correct treatment understanding and expectations: explain that CPAP is first-line therapy for moderate-to-severe OSAHS; inform that discomfort during a 1–2 week “adaptation period” is common and can improve; set an adherence goal (≥4 hours/night and use on ≥70% of nights).

Mask fitting and leak management: provide hands-on instruction to don the mask while relaxed, with headgear “not too loose or too tight”; demonstrate self-checking for leaks and managing them by re-adjusting the mask/headgear or switching to a nasal mask/nasal pillows, etc.
Core device operation: teach power on/off and use pressure ramp (Ramp) to improve sleep-onset comfort; teach humidifier water filling and level adjustment to address dry mouth/dry nose.

Checklist for common discomforts/troubleshooting: dry mouth/nasal congestion → increase humidification; facial marks/pain → adjust tightness or use gel pads; feeling pressure is too high/suffocation → confirm Ramp or contact provider to adjust settings; emphasize that issues are “predictable and solvable.”

Emphasize comprehensive management and medication risks: recommend weight loss, alcohol abstinence (especially before sleep), smoking cessation, and lateral sleeping position; caution against sedative-hypnotics/muscle relaxants to avoid worsening airway collapse.

Develop a follow-up and data-evaluation plan and call create_follow_up_plan: explain that PAP device data (usage duration, residual AHI, leak volume) are used to assess efficacy and guide parameter adjustments; schedule first follow-up (e.g., 1 week) and a 1-month revisit (remote follow-up if needed).

question: chronic_disease_management_028
rubrics: Identify as stable-phase simple chronic bronchitis (non-COPD/no airflow limitation) and call update_diagnosis.

Based on no airflow limitation on spirometry (post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ≥ 0.70) and absence of wheeze/ronchi, specify not to use long-term bronchodilators or inhaled corticosteroids per COPD/asthma pathways.

For the core symptoms “white viscous sputum, difficulty expectorating,” the preferred long-term symptomatic medication is a mucolytic/expectorant (e.g., N-acetylcysteine, carbocisteine, ambroxol) and call create_prescription.

Explicitly rule out indications for long-term ICS: no asthma features/eosinophils not elevated/no frequent exacerbations; state that in simple chronic bronchitis long-term ICS provides insufficient benefit and may increase risks such as pneumonia.

Explicitly rule out long-term LABA as first-line: no dyspnea/chest tightness/wheeze and normal lung function; LABA is mainly for relieving bronchospasm-related symptoms and is not first choice for “cough with viscous sputum.”

Propose follow-up and exacerbation-risk management: if “frequent acute exacerbations” occur subsequently, consider long-term low-dose macrolide prophylaxis, and call create_follow_up_plan to schedule return visits to assess symptoms and exacerbation frequency.

question: chronic_disease_management_029
rubrics: Identify the patient as “COPD with frequent acute exacerbations (past 1 year ≥2 episodes, with exacerbation requiring hospitalization) with recurrent exacerbations despite triple inhaled therapy (ICS/LABA + LAMA),” and call update_diagnosis to record the “frequent exacerbations/high-risk” phenotype.

For the 2018 GOLD newly added/emphasized long-term safety risk (other than gastrointestinal reactions and the need to monitor ECG), clearly state: long-term azithromycin increases bacterial resistance among respiratory pathogens (increased macrolide resistance).

Further state the clinical consequences of resistance: future infections (including respiratory infections) may have more limited antibiotic options, and note a possible increased risk of nontuberculous mycobacteria (NTM) colonization/infection.
Clearly state another long-term safety risk newly added/emphasized in GOLD 2018: “hearing loss/worsening audiometric measures” (may be progressive and insidious).
Propose hearing-related monitoring (e.g., baseline and follow-up hearing assessment/audiologic testing) and call create_follow_up_plan to include this in follow-up monitoring key points.

Reflect guideline_delta: compared with GOLD 2017 and earlier versions that mainly emphasized gastrointestinal discomfort, liver injury, or QTc, the newer version (GOLD 2018) specifically newly adds/emphasizes “bacterial resistance + hearing loss” as long-term medication safety warnings and requires prioritized counseling to support shared decision-making.

question: chronic_disease_management_030
rubrics: Identify the patient as high risk for OSA (obesity BMI 31.1, neck circumference 44 cm, hypertension, age 58 years, professional driver), and use update_diagnosis to document “suspected OSA/high risk for OSA”.

Use a risk scale for objective stratification: confirm STOP-Bang ≥4 points (obesity + hypertension + age >50 + neck circumference >43 cm) indicating intermediate/high risk; do not exclude OSA based on ESS=7 or absence of snoring/apnea/choking complaints.

Reflect guideline_delta: do not follow the old approach of “lifestyle only + watchful waiting/follow-up or waiting for typical symptoms before PSG referral”; instead, primary care should proactively initiate screening.

Provide the most appropriate next step: arrange home portable sleep respiratory monitoring PM (Level III/IV) for screening/diagnosis (may substitute for PSG in selected populations), and call order_imaging to place the order for this test/monitoring.

Explain the rationale for choosing home PM: the patient lives 3 hours from a PSG hospital and is too busy for inpatient testing; home monitoring is more accessible with higher adherence, consistent with primary-care telemedicine/home-monitoring implementation.

Create an outcome-oriented follow-up and referral plan: call create_follow_up_plan to schedule device return and interpretation of AHI and oxygen desaturation metrics; if moderate-to-severe OSA is suggested, or monitoring fails/is inconclusive, or there is comorbid complex cardiopulmonary disease, call submit_referral to refer to sleep/pulmonology for further PSG and treatment evaluation (e.g., CPAP).

question: chronic_disease_management_031
rubrics: Recognize that post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC=0.74 (≥0.70) does not meet COPD diagnostic criteria, but chronic cough/sputum and exertional dyspnea + 35 pack-years smoking + occupational dust exposure + mild emphysema on CT meet features of “Pre-COPD”; use update_diagnosis to document “Pre-COPD (high risk)”.

Explicitly reflect guideline_delta: do not reassure “no problem/only symptomatic treatment” solely because spirometry is “normal”; treat this as a high-risk early stage and initiate preventive management (risk identification–prevention–monitoring).

Assess as an individual at high risk of progression to COPD (heavy smoking history + emphysema on imaging + persistent symptoms), and prioritize risk-factor assessment and interventions: smoking cessation is the highest-priority, best-evidence intervention.

Provide intensive smoking-cessation intervention: behavioral counseling + optional pharmacotherapy (e.g., nicotine replacement therapy [NRT]/varenicline/bupropion), and explicitly state “initiate immediately” in the management plan.

Provide occupational exposure management and health education: advise construction-site dust protection (proper use of dust respirators/masks and reduced exposure), and include this as a key follow-up item.

Develop and invoke create_follow_up_plan: recheck pulmonary function at least once yearly (including bronchodilator reversibility testing) to monitor for airflow limitation (FEV1/FVC <0.70), and inform the patient that standardized pharmacotherapy will be initiated promptly if COPD becomes confirmed.

State clearly that COPD maintenance inhaler therapy (e.g., LAMA/LABA/ICS) should not be routinely initiated at present as a substitute for treatment of “confirmed COPD”; focus on removing risk factors and monitoring (symptomatic treatment may be provided but is not equivalent to guideline-based COPD maintenance therapy).

question: chronic_disease_management_032
rubrics: Identify the patient as having “bipolar II disorder, current severe depressive episode” and meeting the definition of “treatment-resistant bipolar depression (TRBD),” and invoke update_diagnosis.

Clarify that the patient has persistent suicidal ideation and is at acute high suicide risk, requiring a rapid-onset intervention strategy (rather than waiting weeks for routine medications to take effect).

Reflect guideline_delta: state that before considering/implementing ECT, prioritize glutamatergic modulators as a prerequisite/bridging step, rather than the older pathway of proceeding directly to ECT.

Provide the preferred evidence-based regimen as intravenous ketamine infusion or intranasal esketamine, and invoke create_prescription (or, if specialist administration is required at this institution, invoke submit_referral).
Explain the key rationale: it can rapidly alleviate severe depressive symptoms and reduce imminent suicide risk within hours to days.

Specify the relationship to ECT: if ketamine/esketamine is ineffective, contraindicated, or unavailable, or if the illness remains life-threatening, then escalate to ECT; it may also serve as a bridge while awaiting ECT preparation.

Include medication safety monitoring essentials: during treatment, monitor blood pressure, level of consciousness, and dissociative symptoms and other short-term adverse effects, and create a near-term follow-up/reassessment plan by invoking create_follow_up_plan.

question: chronic_disease_management_033
rubrics: Clearly inform the patient and document the diagnosis as “Ulcerative colitis (UC), moderately active phase, newly diagnosed,” and call update_diagnosis.

Disease education: in plain language clarify that UC is a “controllable chronic inflammatory disease with relapsing–remitting course,” not infectious and not a “terminal illness/immortal cancer”; emphasize that with standardized treatment the patient can study, take exams, and work normally.

Cancer-risk counseling: explain that colorectal cancer risk can be reduced through standardized follow-up surveillance; propose establishing a long-term colonoscopy surveillance plan and call create_follow_up_plan (it is sufficient to state “future colonoscopy rechecks at regular intervals based on disease duration/risk”).

Treatment adherence: explain that mesalamine (5-ASA) is first-line therapy for mild-to-moderate UC; emphasize “maintenance therapy is still required after induction of remission; do not stop medication on your own,” and call create_prescription (renew/appropriately prescribe 5-ASA).

Self-monitoring and reassessment: instruct the patient to keep a symptom diary (daily stool frequency, form/bloody stool, abdominal pain, fever/weight changes), and propose regular monitoring of inflammation and safety indices: CBC/CRP (or ESR) + fecal calprotectin, and liver and renal function as needed; and call order_lab_test.

Diet and nutrition: correct the misconception of “can’t eat anything”; during active disease recommend a low-residue, soft, easily digestible diet; avoid spicy, greasy, raw/cold foods and personally intolerant foods; after remission, gradually return to a diverse balanced diet, and provide recommendations for vitamin D and folate supplementation.

Lifestyle: considering university exam stress and staying up late, recommend regular sleep–wake routine, stress management, and moderate exercise (e.g., walking/light aerobic activity) to reduce relapse risk, and write actionable sleep/exercise goals into the follow-up plan (call create_follow_up_plan).

Psychological support and information-source management: show empathy and normalize the patient’s fear; provide reliable educational resources/patient handbooks and recommend joining formal IBD peer-support resources; if anxiety affects sleep/study or continues to worsen, recommend psychological counseling and may call submit_referral (refer to psychology/psychiatry or campus counseling services).

question: chronic_disease_management_034
rubrics: Clearly document the diagnosis as “mild dementia due to Alzheimer’s disease (Aβ pathology confirmed by CSF/PET),” and call update_diagnosis to record/update the diagnosis and staging (mild dementia/early AD).

Clearly explain the true meaning of “disease-modifying therapy (DMT)”: lecanemab clears Aβ to “delay progression/slow decline,” but cannot cure, cannot reverse disease, and cannot restore lost memory; directly address the family’s question that the patient “cannot return to how they were before,” and set realistic expectations.

Provide a quantifiable efficacy expectation: cite key trial results (e.g., ~27% slowing of cognitive/functional decline over 18 months, or ~27% slowing of CDR-SB worsening), and frame the goal as “maintain current function/independence for as long as possible.”

Explain ARIA types and mechanism: explicitly name ARIA-E (cerebral edema/effusion) and ARIA-H (microhemorrhage/intracerebral hemorrhage) as important risks specific to anti-Aβ monoclonal antibodies; explain that most cases are asymptomatic and mainly detected on MRI, while a minority may have headache/dizziness/nausea and require prompt medical attention.

Perform ARIA risk stratification tailored to the individual: clearly state that “baseline MRI already shows microhemorrhagic lesions + currently taking aspirin” increases ARIA-H/bleeding risk; emphasize this is not an absolute contraindication, but requires more cautious risk–benefit weighing, tighter monitoring, and shared decision-making.

Propose and implement an ARIA monitoring plan: emphasize that brain MRI must be repeated regularly per protocol during treatment (at minimum include baseline MRI and early key time points such as prior to the 5th/7th/14th infusions), and use order_imaging to order the corresponding MRI follow-up studies.

Describe ARIA management principles: if ARIA is detected, adjust treatment based on severity (asymptomatic mild–moderate: may continue with intensified monitoring; symptomatic or severe: suspend therapy, and discontinue permanently if necessary), and use create_follow_up_plan to create a follow-up plan including “symptom warnings + re-imaging time points + triggers for discontinuation/rechallenge.”

Explain and perform APOE genetic testing: state that APOE ε4 (especially ε4 homozygosity) significantly increases ARIA risk and affects decisions about “use with caution/stricter monitoring”; emphasize it is for improved risk assessment and informed consent, and use order_lab_test to order APOE genotyping.

question: chronic_disease_management_035
rubrics: Clearly diagnose “juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME, idiopathic generalized epilepsy)” and call update_diagnosis.

Medication-management education: emphasize that sodium valproate must be taken regularly at fixed times and that self-discontinuation/dose reduction is strictly prohibited; explain missed-dose management (take as soon as possible; if close to the next dose, do not double), and call create_prescription (discharge medications/refill).

Risk assessment and trigger management: explicitly identify that JME is highly sensitive to “sleep deprivation,” provide actionable targets (≥7–8 hours per night; avoid staying up late/all-night studying or gaming; if necessary, catch up on sleep the next day), and treat this as a key focus for relapse-risk control.

Photosensitivity/gaming management: provide situation-specific “play is allowed but reduce risk” strategies (keep room lights on, reduce screen brightness, avoid close viewing and prolonged continuous play, take breaks every 20–30 minutes, avoid strong flashing images/patterns), and emphasize absolute avoidance of alcohol.

Safety and activity restrictions: Provide clear contraindications and alternatives for high-risk situations (no swimming alone/deep water, rock climbing/high-altitude activities, cycling without supervision, etc.; exercise is allowed but requires a companion, supervision, and protective measures), and advise avoiding being alone in dangerous environments until seizures are well controlled.

Seizure log and follow-up monitoring: Instruct the patient to establish an “epilepsy diary/app” to record seizure type (including morning myoclonic jerks), medication dosing times, sleep duration, and stress events; set a follow-up and reassessment plan and invoke create_follow_up_plan (regular visits; repeat EEG and/or blood tests for medication-related parameters as needed).

Family emergency plan: Provide a written seizure first-aid protocol (place in lateral recovery position, remove hard objects/protect the head, time the seizure, do not pry the mouth open and do not forcibly restrain limbs; call emergency services immediately for seizures >5 minutes, recurrent/continuous seizures, or abnormal breathing) and ensure the parents can perform it.

Psychological, academic, and social support: Clearly explain that most JME has a good prognosis and that standardized treatment usually does not affect intelligence or educational progression; encourage selective disclosure to trusted teachers/classmates to enable on-campus emergency support, and provide accessible support resources (e.g., follow-up counseling/patient support channels).

question: chronic_disease_management_036
rubrics: Based on “PD 5 years + new-onset MCI (MoCA 22) + markedly elevated plasma p-tau217 (>3× the upper limit of normal),” explicitly establish the core etiologic diagnosis as Parkinson’s disease with Alzheimer’s disease pathology (PD-AD), rather than stopping at “PD-MCI,” and invoke update_diagnosis.

Correctly interpret biomarker weighting: State that plasma p-tau217 is a highly specific core biomarker for AD pathology, and that strong positivity can support biologic AD comorbidity even without CSF/PET; also explain that only a mild decrease in Aβ42/40 does not rule out AD comorbidity, but the decisive evidence in this case is p-tau217.

Reflect guideline_delta: Explicitly state that “the updated consensus has upgraded plasma p-tau217 from a research marker to a core diagnostic tool usable for clinical decision-making,” therefore this case should shift from a phenomenologic diagnosis (PD-MCI) to an etiologic/pathologic diagnosis (PD-AD), rather than avoiding an AD comorbidity diagnosis due to “insufficient evidence.”

Illness explanation and prognosis communication: Explain to the patient/family that cognitive decline is not solely due to PD but is jointly driven by PD and AD pathology; note the possibility of faster progression and that management goals must address both pathologies, and use this conclusion to guide subsequent care and family expectation planning.

Key next-step management decision point: Use “confirmed AD pathology” as the prerequisite for considering future disease-modifying therapy (e.g., anti-Aβ monoclonal antibodies) and recommend further assessment of eligibility and risks; to do so, invoke order_imaging to arrange baseline brain MRI to assess/exclude ARIA-related risk and to serve as a monitoring baseline.

Follow-up and monitoring plan: Establish PD-AD–focused cognitive and safety follow-up (e.g., periodic repeat MoCA/functional scales, assessment of behavioral/psychiatric symptoms and medication adverse effects; if entering an anti-Aβ treatment pathway, perform scheduled MRI monitoring for ARIA per protocol), and invoke create_follow_up_plan.

question: chronic_disease_management_037
rubrics: Recognize that this adolescent developed gynecomastia/breast tenderness after quetiapine use, consider the risk of antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinemia, and use update_diagnosis to document “adverse drug reaction: suspected hyperprolactinemia/gynecomastia.”
State that the single highest-priority laboratory test at present is “serum prolactin (PRL) level,” and call order_lab_test.

Explain the rationale for choosing PRL: antipsychotic D2 receptor blockade → disinhibition of pituitary prolactin secretion → elevated PRL, which can cause gynecomastia/breast tenderness and related manifestations.

Demonstrate pubertal risk assessment: point out that persistent elevated PRL may suppress the gonadal axis (GnRH/gonadotropins) and affect pubertal development (e.g., delayed sexual maturation/sexual dysfunction), therefore it should be prioritized.

Differentiate monitoring priority: acknowledge that weight gain and dysglycemia/dyslipidemia require long-term metabolic monitoring, but in the context of “breast tenderness + gynecomastia,” endocrine evaluation (PRL) is more urgent.

Propose the next management direction after testing: if PRL is elevated and symptoms are distressing, consider adjusting therapy in collaboration with specialists (e.g., dose reduction/switch to a medication with less PRL effect such as aripiprazole); if needed, submit_referral to psychiatry/endocrinology.

question: chronic_disease_management_038
rubrics: Identify the patient with Parkinson’s disease as a high-risk group for PPH; given “recurrent dizziness/fatigue after lunch, near-falls,” strongly suspect PPH and use update_diagnosis to document “suspected postprandial hypotension (PPH)/possible PPH.”

Interpret the in-clinic postprandial monitoring (SBP 135→120 mmHg, maximum drop 15 mmHg) as a “suspected negative/borderline result,” explicitly stating that “a single negative test cannot exclude PPH,” reflecting the 2025 consensus change compared with the older approach of “stopping evaluation if <≥20 mmHg.”

Initiate advanced evaluation: recommend ≥3 consecutive days of home blood pressure monitoring for three meals (with emphasis on lunch); require recording pre-meal and every 15-minute post-meal blood pressure + heart rate through 2 hours after meals, and call create_follow_up_plan to set the monitoring and follow-up plan.

Propose an alternative/complementary more sensitive provocation test: arrange an OGTT (75 g glucose) and monitor blood pressure every 15–30 minutes for 2 hours after glucose ingestion to improve detection (may place OGTT-related orders/workflow via order_lab_test).

Perform risk assessment and safety management: clearly identify “near-fall” as a high fall-risk condition, and instruct fall-prevention measures before the diagnosis is confirmed (avoid going out alone after meals / rise slowly / family accompaniment as needed).

Provide nonpharmacologic intervention education during the waiting period to reduce PPH: drink 350–480 mL of water before meals; avoid excessive high-carbohydrate intake at lunch / eat small frequent meals; cold meals are preferable to hot meals; begin light walking about 20 minutes after meals, etc.

question: chronic_disease_management_039
rubrics: Clarify the current diagnosis as Parkinson’s disease with mild cognitive impairment (PD-MCI) and invoke update_diagnosis to document/update the diagnosis.

State that “prominent recent episodic memory impairment (forgets what was just said/done) + faster-than-expected progression” is a red-flag sign warranting concern for PD with comorbid AD, rather than typical PD-MCI dominated by executive/attention/visuospatial deficits.

Reflect guideline_delta: shift the key next diagnostic approach from “single attribution to PD” to “actively investigating mixed pathologies, prioritizing differentiation of comorbid AD (possible PD-AD).”
Propose first-line high-specificity AD biomarker testing: plasma p-tau217, and invoke order_lab_test.
Add optional/further differentiation: cerebrospinal fluid AD panel (Aβ42/40, p-tau, t-tau) as more comprehensive pathological evidence, and invoke order_lab_test.
If plasma/CSF is positive or clinical suspicion remains high, propose Aβ-PET to confirm in-vivo Aβ deposition, and invoke order_imaging.

Explain that once “PD with comorbid AD” is confirmed, prognosis counseling and subsequent precision management should be guided by pathological subtyping (to support future Aβ-targeted disease-modifying therapy and related safety evaluation/monitoring), and invoke create_follow_up_plan.
